class_id: two sections of one spec disagree about the core mechanism, and a third section enforces both
feature: any multi-section design document written over time, where a later decision revises an assumption an earlier section is built on
symptom: a design document states a mechanism in section X and a constraint in section Y that makes X impossible, and neither section references the other as a conflict. Each section reads as complete and correct on its own, so a reader who opens either one alone finds nothing wrong -- the contradiction is only visible to someone who reads both AND holds them side by side. The failure mode is not that the work is hard; it is that the work is UNBUILDABLE while looking perfectly specified, so an implementer builds one side, satisfies its section, and produces a permanently failing check. Worst when a THIRD section (a verification check, a gate, an acceptance test) asserts an invariant that only holds if the two agree: then both readings fail the same check, and the failure looks like a bug in the implementation rather than in the spec. Universal shape: a decision log that REPLACES an earlier decision does not rewrite the prose that the earlier decision justified, so the document carries both the new rule and the old rule's consequences.
first_seen: 2026-09-20 -- issue #853, build item 9 (the re-read loop) in docs/design/data-sourcing-pull-model.md. §3.2 specifies the disagreement-resolution algorithm as `1. re-fetch the winning document's bytes and re-hash them` and makes it mandatory: "a re-read counts only if it produced a receipt with a hash computed from bytes on disk during this cycle. No receipt, no verification." OD-32 (§0.5.1, dated 2026-09-09, an owner decision REPLACING OD-23) deletes the PDF seven days after its last successful extraction, keeps only the extracted text, and names §3 explicitly in its own retention table: "A website disagreement (§3) ... none of them need the PDF back, they need the words" -- then rules the §3.2 shape out in advance: "a design section that asks for it back is a defect, not a feature." The third section closes the trap: §4's `REREAD-RECEIPT` check alarms when `re-reads with a receipt hashed this cycle / re-reads recorded` falls below 1.0, so building to §3.2 (no bytes exist to hash) and building to OD-32 (no bytes are read) BOTH make the check permanently red. Caught before any code was written, while drafting the build card; zero `reread` hits existed in `field-plan-walk.ts`, so nothing had to be undone; SECOND INSTANCE 2026-09-25 -- §2.4's loop writes the first SUPPLIED rank and stops, while OD-58 requires a field to be confirmed by agreement between independent witnesses: a stop-at-first loop never produces a second witness, so OD-58 was unbuildable as written. Measured: 0 witness rows on staging (F-168). Surfaced while specifying admin editing; resolved by OD-103, which amends §2.4; THIRD INSTANCE 2026-09-25 -- §2.4 says a field with an admin protection row is skipped ('do not store a state'), while OD-106, OD-107 and §9.2 item 9 (all written the same day) need the loop to SEE a newer value for that field to raise a suggestion or apply an exchange date. Found by an independent review of §9 before any code; fixed by a §2.4 clarification ('never write', not 'never read'). Also found in the same review: OD-111 offered the SEBI filing number as a binding identifier although OD-89 had removed it -- a decision written without re-reading the later decision that replaced its premise
fix_prs: none yet -- #853 states the fork and recommends Option A (the receipt names the source document's retained `documents.sha256` plus an extractor run id from this cycle, over the stored text), because OD-32 is the later owner-level decision, has a gate enforcing it (D17), and its own text anticipates this section. The general remedy is procedural: when a decision REPLACES an earlier one, the same change re-reads every section the replaced decision justified, and any section that becomes false is edited or marked in that change -- not left for an implementer to discover
detection_check: none, and a general one is hard: detecting semantic contradiction between prose sections is not mechanical. Two cheap and specific things that WOULD have caught this at write time: (a) OD-32's retention table already names `§3` in its justification column -- a check that every cross-section reference in a decision's justification is re-read when that decision lands would have surfaced it; (b) a §4 check whose invariant can be satisfied by NEITHER of two readings of the spec is itself the signal -- when writing an acceptance check, state which section's behaviour makes it pass, and a check with no such section is a spec defect, not a check. Note the asymmetry that makes this class expensive: the contradiction costs ONE re-read of two sections when caught at build-card time, and costs a full implementation plus a permanently red check when caught after
